text: {"answer":"Nuclear power appears to be an effective low-carbon option, though its costs and delays are contested. The IAEA reports nuclear is a low-carbon source producing about 10 percent of world electricity, and its higher output helped level global CO2 emissions in 2019 [7e88e103d8fb#0]. The World Nuclear Association states that nuclear plants emit no greenhouse gases in operation and that life-cycle emissions per unit of electricity are about the same as wind and one-third of solar [8ef6c9360938#3]. A study of 16 nuclear-generating countries found that cutting CO2 by 1% required a 2.907% increase in nuclear generation versus 4.902% for renewables, suggesting nuclear is more cost-efficient for mitigation [946b45d61e84#0]. The contrary evidence is substantial: an analysis of construction projects found nuclear plants average cost overruns of about 102.5% and the most extreme delays [06384d0fb532#2], and industry commentary notes continuing overruns while renewable costs fall [a518156a3214#3]. A Swedish model also found little cost benefit in rebuilding nuclear once old plants close, given low-carbon alternatives [6b0ccdbcf9aa#1]. Overall, nuclear cuts emissions well, but cost and schedule risks weigh against it.","confidence":62,"one_line":"Nuclear is a low-carbon, emissions-cutting option, but its high cost overruns and delays make it contested versus renewables."}
